summary: This informational memo describes a two-rate, three-color marker used in data services such as Frame Relay and suited to IP and L2 VPN services. It differs from earlier markers in how it handles in-profile traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4115 describes a way for a router to measure a customer's traffic and label each packet green, yellow or red, so that the network can treat the three groups differently. The point of this version is that a packet which is within the rate the customer paid for is coloured green straight away, rather than being checked a second time against a peak rate and possibly discarded.

questions: how does a two rate three color marker work
how do token buckets meter traffic
subtitle: A traffic marker that lets in-profile traffic straight through instead of testing it twice.

tldr.problem: The two-rate three-color marker in RFC 2698 has to run two conformance tests before it can call a packet green, so a packet that is comfortably inside its committed rate can still be dropped at the peak rate bucket, and yellow traffic can starve green traffic.
tldr.mechanism: This marker uses a committed bucket and an excess bucket. A packet that fits the committed bucket is coloured green straight away, one that fits only the excess bucket is yellow, and anything else is red.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo with an IESG note saying it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard and has not been through IETF review for security or congestion control.

facts.label: Authors

today: RFC 4115 is an Informational memo published in July 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It carries an IESG note saying it is not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard, and that the decision to publish is not based on IETF review for security, congestion control, or inappropriate interaction with deployed protocols.

sections.title: What This Marker Is For
sections.content:
The differentiated service defines a quality-of-service architecture for the Internet. Two integral components of that architecture are traffic metering and marking. RFC 4115 describes a two-rate, three-color metering and marker algorithm suitable for differentiated service applications such as IP and Layer 2 VPNs, an algorithm that has been in use for data services including Frame Relay service.

The marker defined here is different from those in RFC 2697 and RFC 2698. It is different from RFC 2697 in that it is a two-rate, three-color marker, where RFC 2697 is a single-rate marker. It is different from RFC 2698 in the way its parameters are defined, which allows better handling of in-profile traffic for predominant service scenarios over a wider range of traffic parameters.

Furthermore, the algorithm eliminates the need for the customer edge device to shape its traffic to a certain peak information rate, as might be the case for the marker defined in RFC 2698 when the value for the peak burst size is smaller than that for the committed burst size. The marker described here operates for both color-blind and color-aware modes, as defined in RFC 2698.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks that sell different levels of service need to measure each customer's traffic and say which packets meet the promise and which do not. This memo describes one way of doing that, and the reason it exists is a fairness problem: a packet that is well within the customer's rate should not be thrown away because of a second, higher test it did not need to pass.

sections.title: Configuration: Rates and Bursts
sections.content:
The operation of the marker is described by two rate values, the committed information rate and the excess information rate, and two burst sizes. The committed information rate and the excess information rate define the token generation rate of a token bucket whose size is equal to the committed burst size and the excess burst size respectively.

The burst sizes are measured in bytes and must be configured to be greater than the expected maximum length of the incoming PDU. The two rates are both measured in bits per second. They can be set independently of each other. Alternatively they can be linked together by defining a burst duration parameter T, where T equals CBS/CIR and also equals EBS/EIR.
sections.plainLanguage: Four numbers describe the marker. The committed rate is what the customer has paid for, the excess rate is what they may use beyond that, and the two burst sizes say how much of each may be sent in one go before the rate is enforced. The two rates can be set separately or tied together by a single burst duration.

sections.title: Metering and Marking
sections.content:
The behaviour of the meter is defined in terms of its mode and two token buckets, C and E, with the rates CIR and EIR and maximum sizes CBS and EBS. The token buckets C and E are initially, at time 0, full, so the token count Tc(0) equals CBS and Te(0) equals EBS. Thereafter the token count Tc is incremented by one CIR times per second up to CBS, and the token count Te is incremented by one EIR times per second up to EBS. The memo's flow chart expresses this as a periodic update of Tc and Te every T seconds.

In the color-aware operation it is assumed that the algorithm can recognize the color of the incoming packet, which may be green, yellow or red. When a green packet of size B arrives at time t, then if Tc(t) minus B is greater than zero, the packet is green and Tc(t) is decremented by B; otherwise, if Te(t) minus B is greater than zero, the packet is yellow and Te(t) is decremented by B; otherwise the packet is red. When a yellow packet of size B arrives at time t, then if Te(t) minus B is greater than zero, the packet is yellow and Te(t) is decremented by B; otherwise the packet is red. Incoming red packets are not tested against either of the two token buckets and remain red.

In the color-blind operation the meter assumes that all incoming packets are green, and the operation is similar to that in the color-aware operation for green packets.

The salient feature of the algorithm is that traffic within the defined CIR is coloured green directly, without the need to pass additional conformance tests. That is the main differentiator from the algorithm in RFC 2698, where traffic is marked green after it passes two conformance tests, those for PIR and CIR. In either color-blind or color-aware mode, the need to pass two conformance tests could result in packets being dropped at the PIR token bucket even though they are perfectly within their CIR, that is, in-profile traffic. Furthermore, in the color-aware mode, the need to pass two conformance tests could make yellow traffic starve incoming in-profile green packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Two counters fill up over time, one at the committed rate and one at the excess rate, and a packet has to fit in a counter to be coloured. The difference from the older marker is that only one counter has to be checked for the common case: a packet that fits the committed counter is green, immediately, and only the packets that do not fit go on to the second test.

sections.title: The Service Scenario
sections.content: The marker can be used to mark an IP packet stream in a service where different, decreasing levels of assurances, either absolute or relative, are given to packets that are green, yellow or red. The memo's example is a service that discards all red packets because they exceeded the service rates, forwards yellow packets as best effort, and forwards green packets with low drop probability. The marker could also be used for metering Layer 2 VPN services such as the emerging Ethernet transport over IP networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The colours are what the rest of the network acts on. A service might throw away everything red, treat yellow as best effort, and give green a low chance of being dropped. The marker itself only decides the colour; what each colour is worth is a decision for whoever is running the service.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says that the security issues resulting from this document are similar to those mentioned in RFC 2697 and RFC 2698.
sections.plainLanguage: The security questions here are the same ones that apply to the older markers, because this document does not introduce anything new in that area.

viz.caption: HOW THIS MARKER DIFFERS FROM THE TWO EARLIER ONES

viz.caption: THE FOUR NUMBERS THAT CONFIGURE THE MARKER

items.title: CIR
items.text: The committed information rate, in bits per second. The rate at which the C token bucket refills.

items.title: EIR
items.text: The excess information rate, in bits per second. The rate at which the E token bucket refills. It can be set independently of the CIR.

items.title: CBS
items.text: The committed burst size, in bytes. The maximum size of the C token bucket. It must be greater than the expected maximum length of the incoming PDU.

items.title: EBS
items.text: The excess burst size, in bytes. The maximum size of the E token bucket, with the same requirement on the incoming PDU length.

items.title: T
items.text: The burst duration, which links the two rates together: T equals CBS/CIR and also equals EBS/EIR.

viz.caption: THE THREE COLOURS AND WHAT PRODUCES THEM

items.label: Within the committed rate
items.desc: Tc(t) minus B is greater than zero, so the packet is green and Tc(t) is decremented by B.

items.label: Beyond the committed rate
items.desc: Tc(t) minus B is not greater than zero but Te(t) minus B is, so the packet is yellow and Te(t) is decremented by B.

items.label: Beyond both rates
items.desc: Neither bucket has room for the packet, so it is red. Incoming red packets are not tested against either bucket and stay red.
